strengths: Introduces and formalizes a new and practically relevant task—high-resolution (up to 2K) instruction-based image editing—which existing diffusion editing methods (limited to ~1K) do not address directly.

The core technical idea, a learnable feature-level transfer function operating on intermediate diffusion features to inject fine-grained details from a high-resolution source into a low-resolution edited reference, is a reasonable and relatively novel test-time optimization strategy that avoids retraining or fine-tuning large models.

The proposed non-overlapping patch synchronization mechanism (blended Tweedie estimates + resampling) is a clever way to reduce patch boundary artifacts while avoiding the computational cost of overlapping-window inference, and the ablation (Fig. 5a, Fig. 7) clearly demonstrates its benefit.

Quantitative results (Table 1) show consistent improvement over four strong diffusion-based super-resolution baselines (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR) combined with a state-of-the-art low-res editor, across both masked and unmasked metrics, and across two resolution regimes (1K, 2K).
Method is shown to generalize across two different backbone architectures (U-Net-based Stable Diffusion and transformer-based FLUX), supporting claims of general applicability.
Reasonably thorough appendix with pseudocode, hyperparameter ablation (τ), synchronization details, and discussion of limitations/societal impact, aiding reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: The evaluation dataset is synthetically constructed entirely from generated (FreeScale-produced) images with ChatGPT-authored instructions and NanoBanana-produced reference edits rather than real-world photographs, which may not reflect true high-resolution editing use cases (e.g., photographs, real texture statistics) and could bias results toward the generative-prior-friendly domain.

Baselines are limited to combining a single low-res editor (NanoBanana) with SR methods; no comparison to other plausible strategies (e.g., tile-based diffusion upsampling/DemoFusion-style approaches, or other recent high-resolution image editing/generation methods such as FouriScale or ScaleCrafter, which are cited but not compared) is provided, leaving open whether SR+edit is really the strongest alternative baseline.

Quantitative gains over the best baseline are relatively modest in several metrics (e.g., M-SSIM 0.739 vs 0.695, M-PSNR 22.114 vs 21.519 at 1K), and no confidence intervals, statistical significance testing, or per-category (object replacement vs. style vs. background) breakdown of the 400 test pairs is reported.

The method requires test-time optimization per image with a moderate number of diffusion timesteps (T=50) and per-patch trainable transfer functions, but no analysis of runtime/latency/optimization iterations or memory scaling with resolution (number of patches) is given, which is important for assessing practicality at 2K and beyond.

The τ hyperparameter (latest timestep for transfer optimization) is tuned via an ablation on only 60 pairs and fixed at 35 as default; sensitivity analysis is limited and it's unclear how robust this choice is across diverse content/instruction types.

Reliance on Null-text inversion for forward-process reconstruction can introduce its own approximation errors and computational overhead, which is acknowledged only implicitly; the interaction between inversion quality and detail-transfer fidelity is not analyzed.

No human perceptual study is included despite editing quality (semantic correctness of instruction-following, aesthetic quality) being difficult to fully capture with HaarPSI/MSE/SSIM/PSNR alone, especially given that fine texture transfer versus semantic content change trade-offs are central to the paper's claims.

strengths: Addresses a practically relevant and under-explored problem: extending diffusion-based image editing beyond the ~1K operating resolution of pretrained models to 2K and beyond, while explicitly motivating why naive 'edit-then-superresolve' pipelines fail to recover source fine-grained detail.

The core technical idea -- a learnable, timestep-dependent 1x1 feature-space transfer function that injects fine detail from a high-resolution source trajectory into a low-resolution-edited target trajectory -- is a reasonably novel way to re-use pretrained low-resolution diffusion priors without any retraining.

The patch synchronization mechanism (blended-Tweedie updates + resampling) is designed to avoid the computational overhead of overlapping-patch inference used in prior tiled-diffusion approaches, and the ablation in Fig. 5/7 shows it visibly reduces seam artifacts.

Quantitative results (Table 1) show consistent improvement over four recent diffusion-based SR baselines combined with a strong low-resolution editor, across both 1K and 2K settings, and qualitative figures show plausible outputs with good detail retention compared to SR-based alternatives.
Demonstrated applicability to two different backbone architectures (U-Net-based Stable Diffusion and transformer-based FLUX), suggesting the method is not tightly coupled to one architecture.

The appendix is unusually thorough, including pseudocode, detailed derivation of the blending/synchronization math, layer-selection strategy, an additional ablation on the hyperparameter tau, and an explicit limitations/societal-impact discussion.
weaknesses: No computational cost analysis is provided anywhere in the main text or appendix. The method performs Null-text inversion (an iterative optimization over T=50 steps) plus per-timestep transfer-function optimization for every one of the N x M patches, which is likely far slower than the feed-forward SR baselines it is compared against; without runtime/memory numbers, the practicality of this 'test-time optimization framework' for 2K+ editing cannot be assessed, which undercuts a central usefulness claim of the paper.

The evaluation benchmark is fully synthetic and self-constructed: source images are generated by FreeScale, downsampled, and then edited with NanoBanana using ChatGPT-generated instructions. There is no evaluation on real photographs or real user edit instructions, and no human/user study of perceptual quality, so claims of practical usefulness for 'real-world' high-resolution editing are not well supported.

The masked reference-based metrics (M-MSE/M-SSIM/M-PSNR, HaarPSI) appear to measure fidelity to the low-resolution reference/source patches, which is exactly what the proposed detail-transfer mechanism is explicitly optimized to maximize; this raises a risk of metric design favoring the proposed method by construction rather than independently validating edit quality or semantic correctness relative to baselines.

Only one backbone (Stable Diffusion v2.1) is evaluated quantitatively; FLUX results are shown only qualitatively (Figs. 5b, 6, with no Table-1-style numbers), so generalization across architectures is not rigorously demonstrated.

The paper does not compare against established patch/tile-based diffusion synchronization methods from the literature (e.g., MultiDiffusion-style or overlapping-window synchronization approaches), which are directly relevant prior art for the proposed synchronization contribution; comparing only to SR-based pipelines leaves the specific contribution of the synchronization module less convincingly benchmarked against the closest related techniques.
Ablation studies are run on small subsets (e.g., 60 image-instruction pairs for the tau sweep in the appendix), limiting statistical confidence in the reported trends.

The claim of 'proposing the high-resolution image editing task for the first time' is somewhat overstated given that patch-wise/tiled high-resolution diffusion generation and SR-for-editing pipelines already exist; the novelty is more incremental (a specific detail-transfer+synchronization mechanism) than the framing suggests.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and, to my knowledge, novel task formulation (high-resolution image editing beyond 1K) with a clear articulation of why naive edit-then-super-resolve pipelines fail (loss of source fine-grained detail conditioning).

The core technical idea—transferring fine-grained details via a learnable feature-space transfer function that aligns a low-resolution edited diffusion trajectory to the high-resolution source trajectory—is a reasonable and creative use of pretrained diffusion priors without any additional training.

The patch synchronization mechanism (blended Tweedie estimates + resampling to avoid needing overlapping inference) is a sensible way to reduce boundary artifacts while keeping compute low; the ablation in Fig. 5/7 convincingly shows visible artifact reduction.

Method is demonstrated on two different backbone architectures (U-Net-based Stable Diffusion and transformer-based FLUX), supporting a claim of general applicability rather than being tied to one architecture.

Quantitative results (Table 1) consistently favor the proposed method across HaarPSI, masked SSIM/PSNR/MSE at both 1K and 2K settings relative to four diffusion-based SR baselines paired with a strong low-res editor, and qualitative comparisons in Fig. 4 show more faithful detail transfer and fewer color/texture artifacts than the SR-based alternatives.

Reasonably thorough appendix with pseudocode, additional ablations (hyperparameter τ), layer-selection details, and discussion of limitations/societal impact, aiding reproducibility of the method's mechanics.
weaknesses: No runtime, memory, or compute-cost analysis is reported anywhere in the paper. Since the method performs test-time optimization of a transfer function per image (with null-text inversion, patch-wise forward/reverse diffusion, and synchronization across possibly many N×M patches at 2K), the practical cost could be substantial; without numbers, it is hard to judge whether the approach is a practically useful alternative to SR-based pipelines or Table 1 baselines.

The evaluation benchmark is entirely self-constructed and somewhat circular: source images are AI-generated (FreeScale) and 'ground-truth' low-res edits used both as the reference conditioning input and (via downsampling) as part of the quality signal come from the same commercial low-res editor (NanoBanana/Gemini). There is no evaluation on real photographs, and no independent human/user study of perceptual quality, which is particularly important for a subjective task like image editing.

The baselines compared against (SR methods applied after low-res editing) are the paper's own strawman construction; no comparison is made to genuinely alternative strategies for extending editing to higher resolution, e.g., directly applying instruction-based editors at their native higher input resolutions where available, or naive patch-wise re-application of the low-res editor without the proposed detail-transfer machinery (only 'w/o Sync' is ablated, not 'w/o transfer function').

Sample sizes for the main quantitative study (400 pairs) and especially the ablation studies (60 pairs) are relatively small, and no variance/error bars or statistical significance are reported, making it harder to assess robustness of the reported gains, some of which (e.g., PSNR margins) are modest.

The method's reliance on a low-resolution reference edit as an unavoidable input means any semantic or structural failure of the low-res editor (e.g., NanoBanana) will propagate directly to the high-resolution output; this is acknowledged as a limitation but not empirically stress-tested (e.g., failure cases are not shown).

The patch-wise synchronization only explicitly handles pairwise adjacent-patch blending along one direction at a time; it is unclear how consistency is maintained at four-way patch corners or across the full N×M grid simultaneously, and no failure-case analysis of large global structural edits spanning many patches is provided.

No code/checkpoint release is mentioned, and given the number of interacting components (null-text inversion, per-timestep transfer function optimization, τ scheduling, blended-Tweedie synchronization), independent reproducibility purely from the paper text may be nontrivial.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated and, to the authors' knowledge, novel task formulation: instruction-based image editing at resolutions well beyond the 1K limit of current diffusion editors, addressing a genuine practical gap between generative editing and real-world high-resolution content needs.

The technical approach is coherent: patch-wise Tweedie-guided optimization of a lightweight per-timestep 1x1 convolutional transfer function in feature space, combined with a synchronization scheme that blends Tweedie estimates at patch boundaries without requiring overlapping-patch resampling, which is a reasonable and efficient design choice.

The method is demonstrated across two different backbone architectures (U-Net-based Stable Diffusion and transformer-based FLUX), and scales qualitatively up to 8K, showing some generality beyond a single generative prior.

Reasonably thorough ablations are provided (synchronization on/off, choice of tau, design of the transfer function/layer placement, real-image evaluation, computational cost breakdown), which aids understanding of design choices and supports the claims about the synchronization module's necessity.
Paper is clearly written with detailed formal derivations (Tweedie estimates, blended latents, resampling) and a full pseudocode/appendix that would aid reproducibility of the core algorithm.
weaknesses: All quantitative baselines (DiT-SR, DiT4SR, PiSA-SR, TSD-SR) are diffusion-based super-resolution methods, not text-driven image editing methods; the paper does not compare against actual high-resolution-capable or naively-upsampled instruction-editing baselines (e.g., running KV-Edit, Step1X-Edit, or ICEdit directly at higher native resolutions, or simple tiled/naive patch application of the low-res editor without the proposed transfer/sync machinery). This makes it hard to assess how much of the reported gain is due to the core contribution versus the fact that SR baselines are ill-suited for editing by construction.

The pipeline depends on an external proprietary low-resolution editing model ("Nano Banana") to produce the reference edit that is then propagated to high resolution; this creates a reproducibility and dependency concern, since the quality of the final result is bounded by, and can inherit failure modes from, this black-box component (acknowledged briefly in Limitations but not analyzed empirically).

Reported computational cost is substantial (full-precision requirement, ~235–635 seconds and ~20GB VRAM per image) yet this overhead is not directly compared side-by-side with the runtime/memory of the SR baselines in the same table, obscuring the practical trade-off versus alternatives.

Evaluation relies solely on automated metrics (masked MSE/SSIM/PSNR, LPIPS, HaarPSI, and CLIP-similarity only in an ablation); no user study or perceptual/human evaluation is included, which is important for editing quality judgments that combine fidelity and instruction-following, especially given the SR-oriented metric suite may not fully capture semantic edit correctness.

Ablation ablation study sample sizes are small (60 image/instruction pairs for hyperparameter and transfer-function design studies), which limits the statistical robustness of the reported comparisons, though the main quantitative table uses a larger 400-pair set.

No systematic failure-case analysis or discussion of when/why the method fails beyond the general limitation statement about dependence on the low-resolution reference and pretrained model imperfections.

strengths: The paper tackles an interesting and under-explored problem: extending instruction-based image editing to very high resolutions (2K–8K) while preserving source fine-grained detail, which existing editing methods (limited to ~1K) and naive SR post-processing cannot address well.

The overall pipeline is technically coherent: patch-wise diffusion trajectory extraction + a learnable per-timestep feature transfer function operating on intermediate U-Net/DiT features + a blended-Tweedie-based synchronization strategy that avoids the computational overhead of overlapping-window inference used in prior tiled-diffusion work.

Reasonably broad empirical demonstration across resolutions (1K, 2K, and qualitative 8K), across two backbones (SD2.1 and FLUX.1-dev), and with ablations on the hyperparameter τ, the transfer-function design, and the synchronization mechanism.
Supplementary material is detailed (pseudocode, derivations for the blended Tweedie / resampling updates, additional real-image experiments, and a frank limitations/cost discussion).
weaknesses: Baseline comparison is structurally biased in the method's favor: all baselines are built by applying generic SR networks on top of the same low-resolution edited reference, whereas ScaleEdit directly conditions each patch's generation trajectory on that same reference through the transfer function. This setup essentially guarantees ScaleEdit will score higher on reference-aligned detail metrics (HaarPSI, masked PSNR/SSIM), and the paper does not compare against other plausible high-resolution editing strategies (e.g., tiled/overlapping diffusion editing, MultiDiffusion/SyncDiffusion/DemoFusion-style patch fusion applied directly to editing, or dedicated high-res generation methods cited in related work such as ScaleCrafter/FouriScale) that would be a fairer test of the proposed synchronization and transfer-function contributions.

The quantitative improvements over baselines are often small (e.g., HaarPSI 0.342 vs 0.335 at 1K and 0.331 vs 0.316 at 2K; LPIPS differences are similarly modest), raising the question of whether gains are within noise given only 400 (image, instruction) evaluation pairs and a single synthetic dataset generated via one editing model (Nano Banana) and one upsampling/downsampling pipeline (FreeScale).

Practical usefulness is undermined by very high computational cost: the method requires full-precision computation, ~20GB VRAM, and 234–635 seconds per image (with Null-text Inversion), which is far more expensive than the SR-based baselines and arguably against the spirit of an efficiency-motivated contribution; the paper acknowledges but does not resolve this.

The method's quality is fundamentally capped by the quality of the externally generated low-resolution reference edit; errors or artifacts in that reference (produced by a third-party commercial model) can propagate directly into the final high-resolution output, as acknowledged in the limitations, but the extent of this failure mode is not quantitatively characterized.

Evaluation of the synchronization strategy (a central claimed contribution) is only shown qualitatively (Figures 5, 9); no quantitative ablation (e.g., boundary artifact metric, seam detection score) is provided to substantiate the claimed benefit over naive non-overlapping patch sampling.

Non-overlapping patch-wise processing is motivated as reducing cost relative to overlapping-window methods, but no runtime/quality comparison against an overlapping-window variant is provided, so the claimed efficiency advantage of the synchronization design is unverified.

The novelty of individual components is incremental relative to existing lines of work: feature-space transfer/injection for detail preservation is conceptually close to existing diffusion feature-injection editing methods, and Tweedie-based blending for patch consistency is related to existing panorama/tiled-diffusion stitching techniques; the paper's positioning as 'the first' high-resolution editing task could be moderated by closer engagement with training-free tiled generation/upsampling literature already in its own related work section.

strengths: Introduces a novel and practically relevant task, high-resolution image editing at 1K-8K resolutions, which is underexplored compared to low-resolution editing methods that cap out around 1K.

The core idea of leveraging existing low-resolution editing outputs as semantic/structural references and transferring fine-grained details from the high-resolution source via a learnable, timestep-dependent feature transfer function is a sensible and test-time-optimization-only approach that avoids costly retraining on high-resolution data.

The patch-wise processing strategy combined with a synchronization mechanism (blended Tweedie estimates + resampling) is a thoughtful solution to the boundary-artifact problem common to tiled/patch-based diffusion generation, and the ablation in Figure 5(a)/Figure 9 convincingly demonstrates its necessity.

Demonstrated generality across architectures (U-Net-based Stable Diffusion and transformer-based FLUX.1-dev) and across a wide range of resolutions (1K, 2K, and even qualitative 8K results), suggesting the method is not narrowly tied to one backbone.

Reasonably thorough experimental protocol: constructed baselines by combining SOTA low-res editing with SOTA diffusion-based super-resolution methods (a sensible strawman given no other high-res editing method exists), used masked variants of standard metrics (M-MSE/M-SSIM/M-PSNR) plus LPIPS and HaarPSI, and reported both 1K/2K synthetic and additional real-image experiments with consistent improvements.

Extensive supplementary material with pseudo-code, detailed derivation of the synchronization strategy, ablations on hyperparameter tau and transfer-function design choices, and candid discussion of computational cost and limitations, which supports reproducibility and transparency.
weaknesses: The method's output quality is fundamentally upper-bounded by the low-resolution reference edit; as acknowledged in the limitations, errors/artifacts from the low-res editing model (e.g., Nano Banana) propagate directly into the high-resolution result, and there is no quantitative analysis of how failure cases in the low-res reference affect final quality.

No dataset or full source code release is mentioned, and the 100 source images plus editing instructions were synthesized/generated by the authors using proprietary tools (FreeScale, Nano Banana, ChatGPT); without release of this benchmark, exact reproducibility of the main quantitative comparisons is difficult for other researchers.

The reported computational cost is substantial (20.29GB VRAM at full precision, and 234.77-635.51 seconds runtime per image at 1K), which is markedly higher than at least one baseline runtime range reported (0.74s), and no analysis is given for how cost scales at 2K/8K, limiting practical usefulness for real applications despite claims of efficiency from avoiding overlapping-patch inference.

The quantitative margins over baselines in Table 1 are often fairly small (e.g., M-SSIM and LPIPS differences on the order of a few percent or less), and no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or user study is provided to substantiate that the improvements are perceptually meaningful rather than within noise.

The comparison baselines are all constructed by the authors (low-res edit + off-the-shelf SR); since no other method natively targets high-res editing, this is reasonable, but it means the comparison space is somewhat narrow and the paper does not compare against any alternative patch-based or tiling-based diffusion synchronization approaches (e.g., MultiDiffusion-style methods) that could serve as more direct ablations of the synchronization contribution.

Only limited detail is given on how sensitive results are to the choice of low-resolution editing model; all experiments use one specific low-res editor (Nano Banana) as the reference generator, so generality of the framework across different low-res editing back-ends is not empirically verified.

The user-facing pipeline requires a separate off-the-shelf low-resolution editing step, meaning the overall system is a two-stage pipeline rather than an end-to-end high-resolution editor; this practical framing/complexity could be discussed more explicitly as a design trade-off in the main text rather than only implicitly.
